flashcards.q: What is the asymptotic path length between two distant sequence positions for an RNN versus a transformer, and what does each cost as a consequence?
flashcards.a: RNN: O(n) sequential steps to connect positions n apart. Transformer: O(1), one attention hop regardless of distance. The transformer's O(1) path costs O(n^2) time/memory for the full attention score matrix; the RNN's O(n) path costs no quadratic term but can't parallelize across time during training.

flashcards.q: Derive why vanilla RNNs suffer vanishing gradients through backpropagation through time.
flashcards.a: The gradient of the loss at step T with respect to hidden state at step t is a product of (T-t) Jacobians, each dominated by the recurrent weight matrix W_hh and the local activation derivative (tanh, max 1.0, decaying away from 0). Multiplying many such factors together shrinks the gradient geometrically with sequence length in the common case, limiting vanilla RNNs to reliably learning dependencies of roughly 10-20 steps.

flashcards.q: Why does gradient clipping fix exploding gradients but not vanishing gradients?
flashcards.a: Clipping rescales an already-too-large gradient down to a bounded norm, which works when the problem is a gradient that's numerically too big. A vanishing gradient is already near zero, so there's no meaningful signal to rescale -- vanishing gradients require an architectural fix (gating), not a training-loop trick.

flashcards.q: Write the LSTM cell-state update equation and explain why it avoids vanishing gradients better than a vanilla RNN.
flashcards.a: c_t = f_t (x) c_{t-1} + i_t (x) g_t -- an additive, gated combination rather than repeated multiplication by a shared weight matrix. When forget gate f_t is close to 1, dc_t/dc_{t-1} ~= 1, so gradient can flow back across many steps largely undiminished (the 'constant error carousel').

flashcards.q: Name the four LSTM gate/candidate components and what each does in one phrase.
flashcards.a: Forget gate: decides what fraction of long-term memory to erase. Input gate: decides what fraction of new info to write. Candidate (tanh, signed): the actual content proposed for writing. Output gate: decides how much of the cell state to expose as the hidden state.

flashcards.q: How does GRU differ structurally from LSTM, and what's the practical parameter savings?
flashcards.a: GRU merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate, and merges the cell state and hidden state into one vector, removing LSTM's separate long-term-memory highway. This gives roughly 25% fewer parameters at the same hidden size (3 gate weight sets vs 4).

flashcards.q: State the two structural reasons transformers replaced RNNs/LSTMs for large-scale sequence modeling.
flashcards.a: 1) Path length: O(1) attention hop between any two positions vs O(n) sequential RNN steps, giving far more reliable long-range dependency learning. 2) Parallelism: RNN step t depends on step t-1 finishing, so training can't parallelize across the sequence dimension; self-attention computes the whole sequence's interactions in one batched matmul, fully parallel across positions.

flashcards.q: What does a transformer trade for its O(1) cross-position path length?
flashcards.a: O(n^2) time and memory for the attention score matrix -- at n=8,192 one head's score matrix is on the order of hundreds of MB at fp16, and at n=100,000 it's infeasible to materialize directly without tiling (FlashAttention).

flashcards.q: When is a 1D CNN still the right choice for a sequence task?
flashcards.a: When the pattern being detected is local and roughly position-independent (phoneme boundaries, ECG motifs, genomic local patterns) and/or when low latency and cheap, parallel, fixed-cost-per-position compute matters more than modeling unbounded-range, content-dependent dependencies.

flashcards.q: When is an RNN/LSTM still the right choice over a transformer in production?
flashcards.a: True streaming with unbounded sequence length and a hard fixed memory budget (RNN state is a constant-size vector; a transformer's KV cache grows linearly with context length), and tiny-footprint edge/embedded deployment where a transformer's attention matrix and parameter count don't fit at all.

flashcards.q: What is the core architectural innovation of Mamba versus classical (S4-era) state-space models?
flashcards.a: Mamba makes the step size and transition matrices functions of the current input token (a 'selective' SSM), letting the model dynamically choose what to remember or forget based on content -- classical SSMs had fixed transition parameters regardless of input, so couldn't selectively attend to content.

flashcards.q: What is Mamba's reported complexity advantage over transformer attention, and what is the current (2026) status of SSMs replacing transformers?
flashcards.a: Linear-time and constant-memory-per-step scaling in sequence length versus attention's O(n^2), with demonstrated benefit on sequences up to roughly 1M tokens on some tasks. Status: an active, promising research direction, NOT a confirmed replacement -- pure SSMs haven't displaced transformers as the frontier LLM default, and much current work builds hybrids interleaving attention and SSM layers instead.

flashcards.q: Why can't gradient clipping alone rescue a vanilla RNN's ability to learn long-range dependencies?
flashcards.a: Clipping only bounds gradients that are too large; it does nothing for gradients that have already vanished to near-zero, since there's no meaningful magnitude left to rescale. Long-range learning requires an architectural gradient highway (LSTM/GRU gating, or attention/SSM), not a training-loop adjustment.
